ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Benefits to farmers from rising market prices 
*181. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
eased to state: 
(a) whether it Is a fact that farmers are not benefiting from rising market 
ices of wheat as the middlemen are taking all the profits; 
(b) whether Government have a plan to ensure that farmers get adequate 
jnefit from higher market prices of their crops; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): ) to (d) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Marketing of wheat along with other notified commodities is 
gulated under the Agricultural Prod uce Marketing Regulation Act(APMC 
:t). The whole geographical area in the State is divided as market area nerein 
markets are managed by the Market Co mmittees. As a msequence of such a 
regulation, the farmer is restricted from  entering to direct contract with any 
bulk buyer, as the produce is required to be inalized through regulated 
markets. The monopoly of the regulated arket has enabled the intermediaries 
operating therein to take a sproportionate share of the price paid by the 
consumer. As per the 'ailable informa tion, the producer's share in the 
consumer's price in major ieat produci ng States varied between 71.1 % to 
85.72%. The balance is

accounted for by charges such as mandi charges, sales tax, weighing charges, 
palledari, brokerage, transport cost and market margins. 
Government has taken several steps to ensure that the farmers get 
adequate benefit from the higher market  price for their crops. These are as 
follows:— 
(i) This Ministry is proactively en couraging the Stat e Governments to 
promote new competitive markets in private and cooperative sectors 
and ailow direct marketing and contract farming programmes by 
suitabiiy amending APMC Act. This is with the objective of 
promoting fair competition, so that the farmers can gain from the 
options available, and take their produce to the centres that offer the 
best prices/services including regulated markets. 
(ii) This Ministry is implementing a capital investment subsidy scheme 
titled 'Construction of Rural Godowns' w.e.f. 01.04.2001, to provide 
the farming community with facilities for scientific storage so that 
wastage and produce deterioration ar e avoided and also to enable it 
to meet its credit requirement without being compelled to sell the 
produce at a time when the prices  are low. The scheme has been 
made farmer friendly by allowing subsidy for smaller godowns of 
50 MT size in general and of 25 MT in hilly areas. Five lakh tonnes 
capacity to be created is reserved for small farmers. Till 
31.12.2005,10932 storage projects having a capacity of 158.68 lakh 
tonne have been sanctioned under the scheme by providing a 
subsidy of Rs. 279.91 crore. 
(iii) Government his permitted futures trading in wheat at the 
commodity exchange to enable farm ers to discover prices of traded 
commodities including wheat well in advance of the crop season 
thus enabling them to decide when to sell his produce. 
(iv) in addition, to ensure payment of remunerative prices to the farmers, 
the Government announces Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for 
major crops. The price support mechanism enables the farmers to 
sell their produce at remunerative prices, whenever the market 
prices tend to fall below the MSP level.

be HIV positive during hospitalisation at SAT Hospital,

Government of Kerala, indicated that the blood given to the child was tested

As transfusion of infected blood and blood prodcts is one of the modes of 
transmission, the National AIDS Control Programme ensures safety of blood 
and blood products before transfusion by enforcing mandatory screening of 
all blood units for transfusion transmissible infections including HIV. If any 
blood unit is found to be reactive to any of the transfusion transmissible 
infections (HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, Syphilid and Malaria), then the 
same is compulsorily discarded on universal safety precautions. Secondly, in 
order to ensure safe supply of blood, professional blood donation has been 
banned in the country since 1st January, 1998. 
One of the principal components of the strategy of ensuring safe blood is 
the promotion of voluntary blood donation. The other activities taken up 
under the programme include modernisation of 1179 blood banks inckftling 
82 blood component separation facilities and adopting quality management 
practices. The strict enforcement of these measures through training and 
periodic monitoring has enabled transmission of HI V through blood, 
reduced from 9% in 1993 to less than 2% in 2005. The goal of the

AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) As per information 
available with the Indian Meteorol ogical Department, the surface air 
temperatures over the Indian subcontin ent show a slight warming trend by 
about 0.4 C during the past 100 years. This warming trend is however not 
uniform either in time or space. Some  seasons do not exhibit as much 
warming trends as the others, and some regions of the country show lesser 
warming trend or even cooling trends. Significant warming trend occur over 
most parts of the peninsular region of the country. Many parts of the North

Report in 2001 has projected that globally averaged surface temperature 
would rise by 1.4 degree centrigrade to 5.8 degree centigrade and the global 
mean sea level may rise by 0.09 to 0.88 m during 1990-2100 in the most

Joining the Indian Ocean Tuna Organization 
1177. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAM Y: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that our countr y has joined the Indian Ocean Tuna 
Organization; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the objectives and other salient features of this organization? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOT C) is a Regional Fisheries 
Organization under the Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) of the 
United Nations. This Organization is mandated to manage tuna and tuna like 
species in the Indian Ocean and adj acent seas. India became a member of 
IOTC from the time it came into existence in the year 1996. Tuna and tuna 
like species are highly migratory and straddling in nature, moving between 
the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) of  adjacent countries and the high 
seas. Hence, cooperative efforts are re quired to conserve and manage these 
resources. Since the objective of IOTC is oriented towards management and 
conservation of tuna and allied resources, India has joined this Organization 
for the sustainable development to tuna fisheries in this region through 
cooperative efforts with the member countries. 
(c) The objective of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission is to review the 
trend of tuna fisheries in the Indian  Ocean and adjacent seas by gathering 
and analyzing scientific information on the resources, maintenance of 
statistics on catch and efforts and maintaining data relevant to the 
conservation and management of the stocks. The Commission is also 
required to coordinate research and development activities in respect of the 
tuna species covered under it and to encourage transfer of technology, 
training of personnel and to address the special interests and needs of the 
member countries. The Commission will promote the objective of optimum 
utilization of the tuna resources based on scientific evidences. At present, 
there are 24 countries represented in the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission and 
the headquarters of the Commission is in Victoria, Seychelles.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) The Seeds Act, 1966 provides the 
framework for regulating quality of certain seeds in the Country Notification 
of a variety is based on the Value for Cultivation and Usage test. Seeds of a 
notified variety can be sold only if they conform to the standards prescribed 
under this Act. The Act also provides for voluntary certification of varieties. 
Certification entails a third party guar antee by an independent agency and 
ensures genetic identity and genetic purity. The Central Seed Committee and 
Central Seed Certification Board an d its various sub committees are the 
agencies set up under the Seeds Act to deal with all matters relating to 
quality control of the seeds. Seed Inspectors notified under the Seeds Act are 
empowered to draw the samples and varify the standards Violation of the 
Seeds Act is a punishable offence. Seed (Control) Order, 1983 another legal 
instrument, has been issued under-the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 in 
order to ensure distribution of quality seeds to the farmers. Seeds (Control) 
Order regulates seed production and distribution. The order provides for 
licensing of seed dealers, the modalities of inspection, sampling, punishment 
of dealers, suspension and cancellati on of licences and has put in place a 
rigorous system of regulation and enforcement. However, the Seed Act and 
the Seed (Control) Order do not apply to farm saved seed.

Essential drugs at cheaper rates 
1210. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will th e Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps Government have taken, so far, to keep its promise of 
providing 354 essential drugs available at cheaper rates as well as to follow 
the Supreme Court's directive to Government that such life-saving drugs do 
not fall out of price control;

during current year as compared to last year in this regard;

this regard; and 
(d) the steps Government have taken in this regard in the interest of the 
common man? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) A Committee 
undor the Chairmanship of Joint Secret ary (PI) was constituted to examine 
the span of price control (including trade margin) in the light of National 
Common Minimum Programme and the observations of the Supreme Court 
in SLP No (C) 3668/2003 and to suggest measures for fulfilling the objective 
of National Common Minium Programme to ensure the availability of life 
saving drugs at reasonable prices. This Committee in its interim report 
submitted to the Government has inter-alia recommended that the National 
List of Essential Medicines 2003 should form the basket for identification of 
drugs under price control. Subsequently a Task Force under the 
Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen was constituted to explore options other 
than price control to make available lif e saving drugs at reasonable prices. 
The Task Force in its report submitted to the Government on 20.9.05 has 
recommended, inter alia that National List of Essential Medicines containing 
354 items should form the basis of drugs to be considered for intensive price 
monitoring, ceiling prices and imposing price control if any. 
In this regard the Indian Drug Ma nufacturer Association (IDMA) has 
represented mainly for freezing all esse ntial drug prices at current levels, 
automatic increase of price upto 5% per annum, Bulk drugs to be kept out of 
price control, removal of Central Excise and other taxes on all medicines, 
review of Essential list after five years etc.

The Government, based on the recommendations of the Committee under 
the Chairmanship of Join t Secretary (Pharmaceuticals) and the Task Force 
under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, Principal Advisor, Planning 
Commission, the Government have drafted a National Pharmaceutical 
Policy, 2006 (Part-A), which has been circulated to various stakeholders 
seeking their comments. Based on the comments received the Government is 
likely to finalize the new Policy shortly. 
Some of the salient recommendations  of the national Pharmaceutical 
Policy, 2006 (Part-A), which contains issues other than statutory price 
control pertaining to schemes for pr oviding accessibility of drugs to the 
common man are: 
1) Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana for the BPL families. 
2) Larger allocation would be made for National Illness Assistance Fund. 
3) State Illness Assistance Funds would be set up in all states with 
financial assistance from Central Government. 
4) Revolving Funds for BPL families would be set up in all the Central 
Government hospitals. 
5) States would also be asked to set up revolving funds in all the 
government hospitals for free treatment of BPL families. 
6) In order to increase the reach of po or people to these funds District 
Level Revolving Fund would also be maintained The quantum of the 
District Level Revolving Fund would be Rs. 1.00 crore and this 
amount would bo provided by the Central Government. 
7) Rajasthan model of Medicare Relief Societies to be replicated in all 
the states.

The important recommendations made in the report of M/s McKinsey &

ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) The di sease is spreading in South East 
Asian countries as well as in Europe & Africa. In Europe, the Avian 
Influenza has been reported in wild birds as well as in poultry. In India also, 
the disease has been reported in Navapur Taluka of Maharashtra and 
Uchchal Taluka of Gujarat. 
Department of Animal Husbandry inform ed that there is no real cause of 
panic, as the disease is localized in the small pocket of Maharashtra, 
bordering the part of Gujarat. The dis ease has been contained in the affected 
areas. All the birds have been culled in the infected as well as surveillance 
zone and disinfection and sanitation process is undergoing in the area. 
142 

[3 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
The Government does not propose to set up a seromonitcring project to 
guard against the menace. However, se ro-surveillance is in progress in all 
the states of the country, including  Orissa. The samples are being taken 
randomly from the birds and are being sent to High Security Animal Disease 
Laboratory, Bhopal. Besides the samples from Navapur, Maharshtra and 
Uchchal, Gujarat, none of the samples have been tested positive for Avian 
Influenza. 
Falling Female Sex-Ratio 
1258. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the female sex-ratio is falling drastically in the 
recent years; 
(b) if so, the reasons for such a decline; 
(c) what will be the implications if such falls is left unchecked; and 
(d) the measures envisaged to check the fall of female children? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) Sex ratio in India has declined over the 
century from 972 in 1901 to 927 in 1991. The sex ratio has since gone up to 
933 in 2001. In contrast the child sex ratio for the age group of 0-6 years in 
2001 in 927 girls per thousand boys against 945 recorded in 1991 Census. 
(b) Some of the reasons commonly put forward to explain the 
consistently low levels of sex ratio are son preference, low value of girl 
child, neglect of girl child resulting in higher mortality at younger age, 
female infanticide, femalo foeticide,  higher childhood mortality and male 
bias in enumeration of population. 
(c) Imbalance in the sex-ratio may lead to further decline in the status of 
women, increase in violence against women practices of polyandry etc. 
(d) Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has undertaken training of 
trainers from State Judicial Academie s to train lower judiciary with the 
objective to'sensitize th e judiciary on the issue. National Inspection and 
Monitoring Committee (NIMC) having representatives of Department of 
Women & Child Development, National Commission for Women, Indian 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [3 March, 2006] 
Council for Medical Research as member s, undertakes periodical visits to 
the districts with low child sex ratio (0-6 years) to oversee the 
implementation of the Act at ground level and monitors the prosecutions 
launched against unregistered bodies and bodies violating provisions of the 
Act/Rules and directions of the Suprem e Court of India in the matter. The 
National Support and Monitoring Cell is being constituted as a mechanism 
to help Appropriate Authorities in apprehending the wrong doer who are 
committing female foeticide/abetting female foeticide. 
It is, however, recognized that mere legislation is not enough to deal with 
thir. problem that has roots in social behavior and prejudices. A number of 
activities to create awareness on th e issue are being undertaken. The 
initiatives include meeting with the organizations working against sex 
selection, involvement of the medical professionals, religions leaders to 
spread the message, requesting police training academies and schools to 
include the issues in curriculum of th eir training, telecasting of video spots 
on private satellite channels and Doordarshan, and involvement of elected 
representatives etc. A 'Save the Girl Child" Campaign with a view to lessen 
son preference by highlighting achievements of young girls has been 
launched. District Magistrates have also been requested to regularly review 
the implementation of the Pre-concepticn and Pre-natal Diagnostic 
Techniques Act along with other health programmes in their district.

1264. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHAR WAL: Will the Minister of

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) In order to improve the existing 
healthcare delivery system and make h ealthcare accessible and affordable to 
the poorer and vulnerable sections of society particularly in the rural areas, a 
National Rural Health Mission was launched in April, 2005. This mission 
seeks to provide effective healthcare to rural population throughout the 
country with special focus on 18 States with poor health indicators and weak 
health infrastructure. Under the strate gy of NRHM, the gaps in the existing 
scenario of rural healthcare is to be addressed through 2.5 lakh Accredited

launched in the year 2004-05 to strengthen capacity of all the States/ UTs for 
Disease Surveillance. The Project aims to strengthen public health 
laboratory services, train personnel  and use information technology in 
surveillance. Early detection and timely response to outbreaks is expected to 
reduce spread of diseases in the population including poorer section of the 
society.

ART to poor patients was initiated by the Government from April, 2004.

Clinical trials 
1274. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to refer to Starred Question 143 
replied in Rajya Sabha on the 2nd December, 2005 and state: 
(a) whether there Is any provision in Schedule-Y which ensure a level of 
safety for clinical trials in India in the context of removal of time lag 
between clinical trials in India and outside; and 
 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [3 March, 2006] 
(b) whether there is any provision in Schedule-Y which provides 
compensation or insurance for the clinical trial patients or their families? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) The amended Schedule Y of the 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act prescribes for submission of adequate safety data 
for regulatory review, before permission is granted to conduct clinical trials. 
Permission to conduct clinical trials for molecules invented outside India 
is granted only when the same trial is being concurrently conducted in other 
countries as well. 
The amended Schedule Y mandates that Ethics Committees review 
"Insurance Policy/Compensation for participation and for serious adverse 
events occurring during the study participation." 
The informed consent checklist under Schedule Y also prescribes that the 
patient should be informed by clinician (Investigator) about "Compensation 
and/or treatment (s) available to the Subject in the event of a trial-related 
injury." 
According to India Good Clinical Practices (GCP) Guidelines, which 
must be complied with as per Schedule Y, the sponsor is responsible to 
indemnify and obtain insurance to cover the cost of treatment in case of any 
study related harm to patients, and also to provide compensation as 
prescribed by the laws of the land.

1300. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that C&AG in its Report No. 9 of 2003 pertaining 
to Railways has stated that large number of existing railway bridges aro

standard of loading than prevalent, i.e., there has been tremendous growth of 
load both in freight as well as passe nger traffic since the construction of 
these bridges;

bridges to handle heavier load of freight and passenger; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) Yes, Sit. It is a fact that presently about 75,600 bridges

constructed to handle loading prevalent at the time of their construction.

section, thorough study is carried out for suitability of existing bridges. If 
required, bridges are rehabilitated/rebuilt to hear the heavier axle load of 
freight/passenger trains.

well laid down system of multi-tier inspection of bridges is followed in the 
Indian Railways. The rehabilitation/ rebuilding of the bridges is carried out 
based on the physical condition as ascer tained during inspection and not on 
the basis of age alone. In case a section is selected for introduction of heavier 
loads, all the bridges of that section are reviewed and strengthened as per 
requirement.

Increase in rail accidents 
†1317. SHRIJANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the numb er of train accidents has increase 
during the last two years; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that  the reason behind these accidents is 
misuse of modem technique by the employees; 
(c) if so, whether Government have taken any steps to minimize the train 
accidents and also to check the misuse  of modern techni que by employees; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (d) No, Sir. Safety is the prime concern of Indian 
Railways and all possible steps are undertaken on a continuing basis to 
prevent accidents. These measures incl ude timely replacement of over aged 
assets, adoption of suitable technologies for upgradation and maintenance of 
track, rolling stock, signaling and interlocking systems, safety drives and 
inspections at regular Intervals to monitor and educate staff for observance 
of safe practices. As a result the number of consequential train accidents 
have come down from 473 in 2002-2001 to 415 in 2001 -2002,351 in 2002-
2003,325 in 2003-2004, and further to 234 in 2004-05.

GOVERNMENT BILL 
The contempt of courts (Amendment) Bill, 2006 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Contempt of Courts Act, 
1971, as passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration." 
(THE VICE-CHAIRMAN, (SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA) in the Chair) 
Sir, I would like to make a brief comment before I request the House 
to take up this Bill. The House is awar e that the existing provisions of the 
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 has been interpreted by various courts and 
judicial decisions to the effect that truth cannot be treated  as a defence to a 
charge of contempt of court. It was the law. Therefore, after a lot of 
discussions in the legal and judicial circle s, it was thought that there is room 
to amend this law and make the truth one of the valid defence. Some eminent 
jurists expressed their views and wrote ar ticles also, and suggested that the 
truth can be a very valid defence subject to the court permitting it. 
I am also happy to inform that the previous Government started this

judiciary is exempted. But it has been done so, just to maintain the 
independence of the judiciary. 
Sir, under the Chapter on Fundamental Rights, every citizen has got 
a fundamental right to speak the truth. If he wants to say anything on the 
matter of inefficiency or the corruption, he is most welcome. Sir, it is not only 
the citizen. We know that once even the Chief Justice of India had said -- he

can't be hauled up for the contempt of court because he happens to be from 
the same community. But the fact is that the ordinary citizen must have a right 
to react. His reaction could be for wrong-doing or his reaction could be for

congratulate the Law Minister  that he has come forward with this legitimate 
amendment of Section 13 of the Contempt of Courts Act.

States of America and the United Kingdom, have the law relating to contempt.

the climax or this is the height of the abuse of this power. This is the

Sir, my humble submission is that even if we accept this 
amendment, the courts would have wide discretionary powers. Of course, if 
derogatory remarks are made to defame th e judiciary, the contemptor should 
be punished. He must be punished. Bu t, Sir, there is an element of non-

system and the deliverance of administrat ion by the system. I would certainly 
request the hon. Law Minister to ponder over this and bring some law to 
introduce the factor of accountability in judiciary also. 
Sir, I would say the ideal situation wojld be when this Contempt of 
Court's Act would be used very rarely. That is because it has to come from 
the heart; whether it is the litigant, whet her it is the media or the politicians,

the judiciary uses this Act the better it would be.

SHRIMATI N. P. OURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I rise to support the 
Contempt of Courts (Amendment) Bid,  2006. Mr, as per the Contempt of 
Courts Act, 1971 if anybody scandalises or lowers the authority of any court 
or interferes with the course of any ju dicial proceedings, he is Sable to be 
punished for criminal contempt and, if there is a wilful disobedience to any 
judgment, decree, direction, order or writ, it is a civil contempt. 
The contempt of court represents a range of offences and those can 
be divided into three broad categories. The first on* it contempt of publication. 
The second one is contempt by disobedience and the third one is contempt in 
the face of the court. 
Sir, there are two main reasons to confer the power on the courts to 
punish people for contempt.  The first one is that the courts should be 
341 

RAJYA SABHA       [3 March, 2006] 
armed with the power to enforce their orders. Secondly, they should be able 
to punish obstruction to the administration of justice. We have imported this 
contempt of court from the British ju risprudence. In Britain, the Law of 
Contempt was evolved by judges themse lves. Later on, they expanded their 
own powers to punish people for acts of scandalising the court. We have 
imported exactly this very phrase from British and put it under Section 2 of the 
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. So, any im putation of dishonesty to judges or 
their judgments is regarded as contempt. 
Recently, the Law of Contempt has  been liberalised in the United 
States of America and the United Kingd om. In the United Kingdom, it was 
liberalised on the recommendations of  the Phillimore Committee to provide 
truth as a defence to a charge of c ontempt. So, India has also started 
amending its Contempt of Court. This cl early shows that the influence of the 
British is still there on our judiciary. 
Coming to the Bill, I would say that, according to the existing 
provision, even the truth of imputation could not be pleaded in defence. Thus, 
if one called a judge dishonest and had evidence to prove it, the courts would 
not allow it on the ground that such an im putation, even if true, would impair 
public confidence in the administration of  justice. The proposed BHi, to some 
extent, covers this because you are inserting a clause, which permits the truth 
as a valid defence. But there is a rider.  The rider is that it should be in the 
public interest. I would like to know what is public interest. The word has a 
very wide meaning. Nowhere, it has  been mentioned as to what constitutes 
public interest. 
The other point I would like to know from the hon. Minister is this. Sir, 
the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution 
recommended the amendment of the Cont empt of Courts Act, since the 
inherent powers of contempt were ve sted with the Supreme Court and the 
High Courts. But, in the Pritam Lai case , the Supreme Court had said that its 
powers of contempt could not be rest ricted by any ordinary legislation, 
including the Contempt of Courts Act. In  the light of this ruling, how is the 
Government going to justify the propos ed amendment? Is it going to bring 
amendment to the relevant articles -- articles 129 to 142 -- so as to set aside 
the judgement of the Court in the Pritam Lai Case? I request the hon. Minister 
to reply to this question. 
Finally, Sir, I would say that there are inconsistencies in looking at 
and deciding the contempt cases.   For example, the Supreme Court in the 
242 

[3 March, 2006]                RAJYA SABHA 
Arundhati Roy case has pronounced one day's imprisonment with a fine of 
Rs. 2,000, in a contempt case. In 1997, a Chandigarh-based professor was 
imprisoned for six months for making derogatory remarks against a former 
Chief Justice of India. At the same ti me, there were others similarly placed 
who were either ignored or got away with just having been reprimanded. Dr. 
Kiran Bedi committed contempt of court when she failed to submit an 
undertrial's medical report to the Supreme Court. A former Law Minister 
called judges 'rotten eggs'. A former Chief Minister escaped from the 
contempt in spite of ma king contemptuous utterances. So, the common man 
is unable to understand as to which on e amounts to contempt of court. Even 
in England the Contempt law has hardly been used for more than the last 
seven decades. 
Speaking on the-use of this Law, Lord Denning observed, "Let me 
say, at once, that we will never use this jurisdiction as a means to uphold our 
own dignity". If such power is necessary for preserving the public confidence 
in the judiciary, then the same argument would hold good for preserving 
confidence in the Government, its bureaucracy and police. After all, these are 
also performing public functions and it is equally important for their efficacy 
that public confidence in them should also be preserved. So, I would suggest 
that the best check against their degener ation was their accountability to the 
people for which it was essential that the people should have the right to 
freely comment on them and criticise them. 
So, I would suggest that the Government should streamline or 
repeal this outdated piece of legislati on to protect the freedom of speech and 
expression provided under article 19 of the Constitution to every citizen.

The Girl Child (Elimination of Discrimination and Violation of Rights and 
other Welfare Measures) Bill, 2003 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Mr. Deputy Chairman, 
Sir, I move: 
That the Bill to eliminate the discrim ination against the girl child by 
providing for the equal upbringing and remove of neglect by her 
parents or guardians and violation of her rights by marrying her off 
during her childhood and forcing her in begging, prostitution and 
other crimes by providing deterrent  punishment for such violations 
and for welfare measures such as free and compulsory education 
including vocational education enabling her to enjoy her childhood 
and for matters connected therewith and incidental thereto, be taken 
into consideration. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA) in the Chair} 
Sir, it is a national shame that the girl child is the most unwanted in 
majority of the families of our nation who prefer to eliminate even the foetus if 
it is of a girl child. Thousands of legal or illegal ultrasound clinics are 
functioning in the country, which are in famous as pre-birth sex determination 
test clinics. As happens in our Indian  households, everybody wants a male 
baby and for this the services of the sex determination clinics are taken. If the 
foetus is that of a female, it is abor ted as soon as possible. For this the 
consent of the mother is neither taken nor it is respected. In some cases, it is 
the mother who decides to eliminate the female foetus. This is common not 
only in illiterate poor families  but it is more in educated and affluent families. 
In western countries, ultrasound is used to find out the deformity in the child 
to safeguard the child as well as t he mother, but here in India they use 
ultrasound clinics-to find out whether it is  a female foetus so that Itt can be 
aborted. Though prenatal se x determination is illegal in the country, but who 
bothers about the law. This  profitable nefarious bus iness is increasing by 
leap and bounds resulting in steep decline in male-female ratio in the 
country, particularly in the northern and western regions of the country. 
Sir, today, 16 States, more specific ally, 70 districts and 23 cities in 
the country, have a shocking sex ratio. If this is not taken seriously, 15 years 
later, the effect of what we see today will surface as a social unrest.
